title: Chapter 46: Rowan Writes Back, Part 3 of 5: Fingernail-Small
html:
Juno came back at the first bell after noon.
She came down the three steps into the crypt slowly, on the sides of her feet, with the snow on her cap and her shoulders, and her face not red any more but white, the way faces go white when the cold has got past the skin. She did not come down the hall to the side vault. She stopped just inside the door, and leaned against the wall there, with her eyes shut, and breathed.
Lyra was beside her before she had taken three breaths.
"Did he come?"
Juno did not open her eyes.
"He came." She breathed. "At noon. Exactly. On his own. Not with the others. He came down Gallows Lane from the Ministry end, walking fast, with his collar up, and he didn't look at me. He went past the pump and stopped at the horse trough on the other side and bent down like he was fixing his boot." She breathed again. "And when he stood up again there was something on the edge of the trough. And he walked away."
She put her hand inside her coat.
She took it out closed, and held it out to Lyra, and opened it.
It lay on her red palm in the middle of the wet wool of her mitten. Small. White. Hard. A square of folded paper no bigger than a fingernail. So tight, and so neat, and so sharp at every corner, that it looked as if it had been carved.
Lyra did not take it.
She stood by the door of the crypt and looked at it. And she knew it. She had never seen one before, not one of his, not with her own eyes. But she had heard Corin talk about them, and Oren, and she had read about them in the Ledger, in Corin's square capitals, three times. Kross folds like that. His wrappers. Small. Very small. Into a hard tight square. And Wren's, on Corin's knee this morning, before he opened it.
And Rowan's. Rowan's, that Corin carried in the Ledger. I will. A sweet wrapper folded into a tiny square on the night of the tenement, and dropped on a step, and picked up. She had seen that one. On the barge. She had held it on her palm, the way Juno was holding this one now, and turned it over, and felt her throat close.
This was the same.
This was the way a man with long careful fingers had taught a frightened boy to fold paper, on his first day, at a desk, to keep his face still.
She took it off Juno's palm.
It was cold. It had been in the snow, on the edge of a horse trough, and then in Juno's mitten for an hour. It weighed nothing at all.
"Thank you," she said.
"Open it," said Juno. Her eyes were open now. "I didn't. I wanted to, all the way, and I didn't. Open it."
Lyra went to the nearest lamp, on its bracket on the first pillar, and held the little square up under it.
It did not want to open. It had been folded too well. She picked at the corner with her thumbnail, the way Corin had picked at Wren's, and it did not come. She tried again. Her hands were shaking. She made them stop. She tried a third time, very slowly, and the corner lifted, and she began to unfold it.
One. Two. Three.
She counted without meaning to. She had always counted. Steps. Bells. People. Memories.
Four. Five. Six.
It was not a sweet wrapper. It was paper. Thin, cheap, gray-white paper, torn from the back of something. A drill book, perhaps. A cadet's notebook. There were faint blue lines on it.
Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten.
Eleven.
It lay open on her palm, in the yellow lamplight. A torn square of thin gray paper the size of a playing card, creased and creased and creased into a hundred tiny diamonds by the folding, so that it looked like the skin of something.
There were five lines on it. In pencil. In a hand she knew.
She had not seen it for two years. She had not seen it since he was fourteen, sitting at the long table in the schoolroom at Crown Walk, with his tongue between his teeth, writing out his Latin verbs for the tutor and blotting them with his sleeve. It had been a boy's hand then. Big, and round, and sloping all over the place, with ink on every finger.
It was not a boy's hand now. It was small and tight and upright and very even. The hand of somebody who had been taught. Who had sat at a desk for two years with someone standing behind him, and been told, gently, kindly, again, until every letter was the right size.
But it was his. She knew it the way you know a voice through a wall. The R at the end, with the little hook on its tail that he had always done, ever since he was six, because he thought it looked like a sword.
St Bride's.
The bell tower. Today. Second bell after noon.
Alone. If anyone is with you I will not come up.
I have one question.
R.
Lyra read it three times.
Then she stood very still under the lamp with the little gray paper on her palm and felt the floor of the crypt tilt under her feet, very slowly, like the deck of a barge in the wind.
St Bride's.
"He knows," she said. "He knows where we are."
Juno had come up beside her. She was looking at the paper too, on her toes, over Lyra's arm.
"I didn't tell him," she said at once. "I didn't. I never said a word. I said from your sister and that's all. I swear it on Gran."
"I know you didn't."
"Then how—"
"I don't know." Lyra looked at the five lines. At the R with its little sword. "Maybe he doesn't know. Maybe it's only—" She stopped.
Because she had remembered.
Not a memory. Not one of the four she had left, that she counted at night like coins. Something smaller. Something that had been folded away so long at the back of her that she had not known it was there until this moment, under the lamp, with his writing on her palm.
A Midwinter morning. Very early. Dark still. Snow. Two children in their best coats, one big and one small, standing in a graveyard among black trees, holding their mother's hands. One on each side. And the mother looking up. At a square tower, black against the snow, with a clock on it. And the clock had stopped.
Twenty past four, the mother had said. In her voice that went up at the ends of things, the voice that counted a hundred brush strokes in a language Lyra did not speak. It has been twenty past four in this tower since before I came to this city. Since before your father was born. Isn't that a fine thing? A place where it is always the same time.
And the small one, the boy, had said: Can we go up?
And the mother had laughed, and said: One day. When you're big. When you need a place to be.
Lyra stood under the lamp.
She had not known that was there. She did not know where it had come from. It had not been one of the four. It had been folded away so small, under everything, that the Duke of Marrow had not found it, and nobody had sold it, and nobody had burned it. And now it was here. Open on her palm. Like his letter.
"He doesn't know we're here," she said slowly. "He doesn't know anything about the crypt. He chose it because—" She looked at the paper. "Because she brought us here. Once. When we were small. And said that one day, when he was big, he could go up."
Juno did not say anything. She looked at Lyra's face for a long moment, and then looked away, at the floor, the way Gideon looked away from things.
Lyra folded the paper again.
She did not fold it his way. She could not. She folded it in half, and in half again, like a letter, and put it inside her coat, against her chest, where Rowan kept hers.
Then she went to tell Corin that she was going up the tower alone, and that he was not to argue. But on the way, she stopped at the far brazier, where the doctor had gone back to sleep against his pillar after his rounds.
The Letter She Kept
There were three quarters of a bell before the second bell after noon. She had counted. She sat down on the floor by the brazier, with her back to the next pillar along from the doctor's, and took her own letter out of her coat.
The one Rowan had given back. Unopened. A page torn from Hessa's ledger, with the faint blue lines and the red margin. Folded in three. Ro. Soft and creased from a week in Juno's coat, with a brown stain at one corner that she thought was tea from the barge, and hoped was.
She had not meant to open it. It was his. Even if he had given it back, it was his. She had written it for him.
She opened it.
It was strange, reading your own hand. Like hearing your own voice through a wall. She knew every word before she read it, and still the words surprised her. She had written it on the barge, at the long table, by Hessa's lamp, a week ago, on the night Juno came with the catalogue. Her hand had been shaking. She could see it. The letters went up and down the blue lines like a boat on choppy water.
Ro. It's me. I'm alive. Father's alive. I can explain everything, if you'll let me.
That was the beginning. She had remembered that much. She had not remembered the rest.
There was a great deal of the rest. Both sides of the page, and squeezed up the margins, and round the corners, in smaller and smaller writing as she ran out of room. She read it now, slowly, by the red light of the coals, with the smell of pears in the warm air round her and the children breathing on their pallets.
It was all explaining.
Every line of it. Where she had been. Why she had gone. What Aunt Cressida had said, and why it was not true. Why she had not come to the Academy. Why she had stopped writing. What she had done since. Who she was with, and why they were good. It went on and on, line after line, round the corners and up the margins, and every line said the same thing in a different way.
It wasn't me. Please believe it wasn't me. Please don't hate me.
She read it all.
Then she sat with it on her knee for a long time, and looked at the coals.
He had not needed it. That was what she understood, sitting there. He had given it back to her unopened, and said I can't carry two, and she had thought, when Juno told her, that it meant he did not want it. That he did not want her. And it did not mean that at all. He had kept the old one. The one from a year ago, that he had carried against his skin since the night he fought a boy by the cadets' stove. He had not opened that one either.
He did not want her explanations. He had had two years of explanations. From Aunt Cressida in the hall. From the Inquisitor in his warm room. From the sergeant with the stick and the boys on the bench who stopped talking when he came in.
He wanted one question answered.
And she did not know what it was. And nothing in this letter, not one line of it, round all its corners and up all its margins, was the answer. She was sure of that. She did not know how she was sure.
She folded the letter again. In three. The way it had been.
She held it over the brazier.
The heat came up off the coals into her hand, and the edge of the paper began to curl, very slightly, and go brown, the way the edge of a leaf goes brown in autumn. She held it there. It would be easy. One more inch. The coals would take it, and it would go up in one quick yellow flame, and all the explaining would go up the chimney of the crypt into the snow, and nobody would ever read it.
She did not move her hand the last inch.
She thought about Father. Lying in the hay in the barge, with Hessa's blanket over him, tapping. For two years. The same thing. Over and over. Four, two, nine, three. Not explaining. Not saying it wasn't me or please believe or I can explain everything. Just sending the same four numbers, again and again, to anybody who would listen. And waiting.
That was all he had. Four numbers, and the waiting.
And she had a whole page of words. Both sides. Round the corners.
She took the letter away from the brazier.
She did not burn it. She put it back inside her coat. Not against her chest, where she had put Rowan's. In the other pocket. The outside one. Where you keep things you might need to give away.
If he doesn't come, she thought, I'll give it to Father. I'll read it to him. All of it. Round the corners. He won't know what it means. But he'll hear somebody's voice saying a great many words, slowly, for a long time, to him. And that might be something.
She got up.
And as she got up, she looked down, without meaning to, at the nearest pallet. At the little girl on it. Polly. Six years old, lying on her side with her face still wet from the morning's washing, watching the lamp on the pillar the way she had watched it all day, all week, without blinking.
Polly blinked.
Lyra stopped.
She stood very still, with her hand on the pillar, and looked down. And Polly's eyes, which had been on the lamp, had moved. Not far. A little. From the lamp to the brazier. To the red glow of the coals, where the edge of a letter had been held, and curled, and nearly burned, and been taken away.
And then, slowly, from the brazier, up.
To Lyra's face.
They rested there. The way Wick's had rested there, by the brazier in the arches. The way Gideon's had rested on Juno's, on the step. For a moment. Two moments. As if there was somebody there.
Then they went back to the lamp.
Lyra did not breathe.
She stood there for a long time. Polly did not look at her again. She lay on her side and watched the lamp, and her eyes were open and still, and she did not blink.
But she had.
"Doctor," said Lyra. Very low. Not to wake him. To tell somebody. "Doctor. She blinked."
Silas did not wake. He slept on against the pillar, with his chin on his chest and his crooked spectacles crooked, and one boot on.
But Mrs. Doyle, coming down the hall with her jug and her loud kind voice, had heard. She stopped by the pallet, and looked down at Polly, and then at Lyra's face. And her big red cheerful face did something that Lyra had not seen it do all week. It went quiet.
"Did she, my lady," said Mrs. Doyle. Softly. "Did she now."
And she knelt down, with a great creak of her knees, and wet her cloth, and began to wash Polly's face again. Very gently. Talking to her the whole time. There's my lamb. There's my good girl. You blinked for the lady, didn't you. You blinked.
Lyra went to the side vault, to tell Corin she was going up the tower alone.
The Tower
Corin did argue. But not for long.
He lay on his bench under the skulls and looked at the five lines on the little gray paper, which Lyra had unfolded again and held out for him to read, and he read them twice, and then he looked at her, and she looked back at him. And whatever he saw in her face, he stopped.
"Oren," he said instead.
"No."
"Not in the tower. At the bottom. In the porch. Out of sight." His gray hand was flat on the Ledger. "If anybody comes up the hill after him. If anybody comes into the graveyard who isn't him. Oren sees. That's all."
Lyra thought about it.
"At the bottom," she said. "Not in the porch. In the crypt door. Where Rowan can't see him from the path."
"Yes."
"And if he comes alone, Oren doesn't move. Not for anything. Not if he hears me shout. Not if he hears me cry."
Corin was quiet for a moment.
"Yes," he said.
Oren, in the arch of the vault, did not say anything at all. He took Terrence's coat down off the hook, and put it on, and went to stand in the crypt door.
The door into the tower was in the porch of the church.
Lyra had not noticed it before. You would not, unless you were looking. A narrow door of black oak, so old that the wood had gone silver at the edges, set into the stone wall of the porch beside the big church doors, where the stone bench was. It had a ring handle of black iron, and a keyhole, and no key. And it was not locked. When she turned the ring it lifted, stiffly, with a groan, and the door came open toward her an inch, and stopped, and she had to put her shoulder to it.
Cold air came out. Colder than the snow. Old, still, stone-smelling air, that had been shut up in the dark a long time.
She went in, and pulled the door to behind her, and stood at the bottom of the stair.
It went up in a tight spiral, round and round a stone pillar in the middle, like the inside of a shell. The steps were wedges of stone, narrow at the pillar and wide at the wall, and worn into hollows in the middle by five hundred years of feet. There was no rail. There was a rope, instead, fixed to the wall with iron rings, black and greasy and hard with age. There was no light, except what came in through narrow slits in the wall, every twenty steps or so, slits no wider than a hand, with the snow-light coming through them gray and thin and lying on the steps in long pale stripes.
She began to climb.
One. Two. Three.
She counted. Of course she counted.
Forty. Forty-one. The first slit. She looked out of it as she passed. The graveyard, below, white. The bent black yews. The path between the graves, trodden gray. Nobody on it.
Eighty. The second slit. The roofs of the city, going down to the river. Smoke.
At a hundred and four, the stone stair stopped, and there was a wooden floor over her head with a square hole in it, and a ladder going up through the hole.
She climbed the ladder.
She came up through the hole into a small square room, as high as it was wide, with walls of bare stone and a floor of rough boards, gray with dust and white with the droppings of birds. There were pigeons. She heard them before she saw them, a soft uneasy muttering up in the dark under the roof beams, and the clap of wings, and then a feather came down past her face, turning, slowly, gray, and landed on the boards.
And in the middle of the room, the clock.
Not the face. The face was outside, on the other side of the wall, where people could see it. This was the inside. The works. A great iron frame, as tall as a man and as wide as a cart, black with old grease and red with rust, standing in the middle of the floor on four iron legs bolted to the boards. And inside the frame, wheels. Wheels within wheels. Big ones, as big as a cartwheel, with teeth like a saw. Little ones, the size of a coin. Rods, and bars, and levers, and a long iron arm that went up from the top of the frame to the wall, where it disappeared through a hole toward the face outside. And hanging down from the bottom of the frame, on chains as thick as her wrist, into a long dark slot in the floor, two great iron weights, like coffins, that had come all the way down to the bottom of their chains a long time ago and stopped there.
Nothing moved.
It was so still, that great black iron thing, that it made the room feel stiller than an empty room would have felt. As if somebody had been holding their breath in here for a hundred years.
She walked round it.
On the far side, set into the wall at the height of her head, there was a small round window of thick greenish glass, like the bottom of a bottle. The light came through it green and wavering. And next to the window, where the long iron arm went through the wall, there was a little brass dial, the size of a saucer, with two brass hands on it. A small copy of the face outside, so that whoever kept the clock could see what the big one said without going out to look.
Twenty past four.
She stood and looked at it.
It has been twenty past four in this tower since before I came to this city. Isn't that a fine thing? A place where it is always the same time.
She put out her finger, and touched the brass dial. It was so cold it burned.
There was another ladder in the corner, going up through another hole in the ceiling. She did not climb it. She could see, through the hole, what was up there. A great dark shape, hanging, filling the whole of the space above. The bell. Green with age. Huge. Its mouth open downward over the hole like the mouth of a cave. And a rope coming down from it, through the hole, past her, through another hole in the floor at her feet, down into the dark, all the way to the bottom of the tower, where somebody pulled it.
She had heard it every hour since Wednesday. The bell of Saint Bride's. It rang the hours even though the clock had stopped, because an old deaf man called Amos, who swept the church and dug the graves, listened for the Ministry's bell across the river, and when he heard it, he pulled the rope. Silas had told her. He's been doing it for forty years. He can't hear a word you say to him. But he can hear the Ministry's bell from the bottom of a grave.
She sat down on the dusty boards with her back against the stone wall, under the little green window, beside the stopped clock, and waited.
It was very cold. Colder than the graveyard. Colder than the Steps on Wednesday morning. The cold came off the stone into her back, and up off the boards into her legs, and in through the round green window in thin wavering bars of light that had no warmth in them at all. Her breath went up in front of her face and hung there. The pigeons muttered in the dark.
She took the little gray paper out of her coat and unfolded it and read it again.
Alone. If anyone is with you I will not come up.
I have one question.
She did not know what the question was.
She had thought about it all the way up the hundred and four steps, and she had thought of a hundred questions he might ask, and she did not know which one it would be. Why did you do it? Why did you let them take the house? Why did you leave me at the Academy and never come? Why did you let them take Father? Where have you been? She had an answer for every one of them. She had had answers for two years. She had written them out a hundred times in the little cold room under the roof, in letters that he kept and did not open.
She did not know if any of the answers were enough.
The pigeons stopped muttering.
All at once. As if somebody had put a hand over their beaks.
And in the silence, far below, at the very bottom of the tower, Lyra heard the black oak door groan open on its hinges, and stop, and groan again as somebody put their shoulder to it.
And then footsteps on the stone stair.
Quick. Light. Even. The footsteps of somebody who had been taught to climb stairs a certain way, at an Academy, by a sergeant with a stick. Coming up. Round and round the stone pillar in the middle, like the inside of a shell. Not stopping at the slits.
She stood up.
She did not know why. She stood up off the boards with her back against the cold wall and the little gray paper crushed in her hand, beside the stopped clock, under the round green window, and listened to her brother coming up the tower to her.
Forty. Sixty. Eighty.
And then, somewhere above her head, in the dark, the great green bell moved.
She felt it before she heard it. A shiver in the air. A trembling in the boards under her feet. The rope beside her, the one that went down through the floor to old Amos at the bottom, jerked, and went taut, and the bell swung.
And spoke.
It was not a sound. It was too big to be a sound. It came down through the hole in the ceiling and filled the little room the way water fills a jar, all at once, to the brim, and went into her bones, and her teeth, and the backs of her eyes. The iron clock rang with it. The boards rang. The stone walls rang. The pigeons burst up from the beams in a gray storm of wings and went round and round the little room and out through some gap under the roof. And Lyra stood with her back against the shaking wall and her hands over her ears and her mouth open, and could not hear herself.
Once.
And again. Twice.
The second bell after noon.
Then the great bell swung back, slowly, and hung, humming, and the hum went down and down and down, through the boards, through her feet, into the stone, and was gone.
And in the silence it left, very loud, she heard the ladder creak.
And a hand came up through the square hole in the floor, and took hold of the edge of the boards. A long hand. Thin. With the knuckles scraped.
